en: The Sūtra on Purifying Karmic Obstructions, translated by an unknown master and now appended to the Qin records.
Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was staying at the Āmra Grove in Vaiśālī, together with a great [assembly].

The assembly consisted of five hundred bhikṣus and thirty-two thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Their names were: Bodhisattva Destroyer of Māra, Bodhisattva Radiant Play of Supernatural Powers, Bodhisattva Lotus Body, Bodhisattva King Who Emits Light, Bodhisattva Constantly Disciplined Body, Bodhisattva Fulfilling the Vows of the Multitude, Bodhisattva Firm Resolve Adorned with Jewels, Bodhisattva Variegated Flower Eye, Bodhisattva King of Pure Sound, Bodhisattva Illuminating Light, Bodhisattva Wondrous True Gold, Bodhisattva Subduer of All Sense-Organs and Their Objects, Bodhisattva Great Thunderous Sound, Bodhisattva Accumulation of Wish-Fulfilling Light, and the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī. These thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas served as the leaders of the assembly.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Vimalaprabha who entered the city of Vaiśālī to beg for alms in due order; not knowing [the householder's identity], he entered the home of a courtesan.
When Vimalaprabha had entered her house, the courtesan conceived a defiled mind toward him and thought to herself:
"I must now certainly engage in sexual union with this bhikṣu."
"If you do not comply with me, I shall take my own life.
Having thought this, she immediately closed the door and said to the bhikṣu,
"I wish to engage in sexual intercourse with the Venerable One."
"If you do not comply with me, I shall surely die.
Then Vimalaprabhā said to the courtesan, "Stop! Do not do this."
Sister! I should not now commit such an act. Why is that?
"The precepts ordained by the Buddha are what I must practice; I would rather sacrifice my body and life than violate these precepts.
At that time, the courtesan thought again:
"I shall now use incantations and medicinal herbs to cause this bhikṣu to engage in sexual acts with me."
He said to the bhikṣu, "I cannot now cause you to regress or violate the prohibitive precepts; you should simply accept the food I offer.
He then entered the house, incanted the food, and threw it into the bhikṣu’s bowl.
By the power of the incantation, this bhikṣu immediately lost his right mindfulness, and lustful thoughts arose within him, increasing and intensifying further and further.
At that time, seeing the bhikṣu’s countenance change, the courtesan stepped forward, took his hand, and engaged with him in sexual acts.
At that time, after the bhikṣu had engaged in sexual intercourse with that courtesan out of mutual passion and delight, he took the alms-food he had collected and returned to the monastery.
Upon arriving at the monastery, great remorse arose within him and his entire body was feverish with distress:
"Alas! What a tragedy!"
"What is it to have one's great precepts violated?
I should no longer accept the faithful offerings of others; I am now a person who has broken the precepts and shall fall into hell.
Then, Vimalaprabha spoke these words to the bhikṣus who were his fellow practitioners of the holy life:
"I have now broken the precepts; I am no longer a śramaṇa and shall surely go to hell.
At that time, the bhikṣus asked Vimalaprabha, "What were the causes and conditions by which you broke these precepts?"
Then Vimalaprabha recounted the aforementioned events in detail.
At that time, his fellow students said to Vimalaprabha:

"Virtuous one, you should know that there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Mañjuśrī who has attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). He is well able to eliminate the offenses of breaking the precepts and also causes sentient beings to be free from all hindrances and entanglements."
"I shall now go with you to the place of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī to dispel your grief and remorse.
At that time, Vimalaprabha had still not eaten; he and the bhikṣus went to the place of Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince.
Having arrived, he paid his respects, made offerings, and showed reverence, then reported the aforementioned matter in detail to Mañjuśrī.
Mañjuśrī said to Vimalaprabha, "Eat now."
"After we have finished eating, we should go together to the place where the Tathāgata is and inquire about this matter;
as the Buddha explains it, we shall all together receive and uphold it.
Having finished their meal, the bhikṣus went with Mañjuśrī to the place where the Buddha was.
Having arrived, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the bhikṣu Vimalaprabha was filled with fear and did not dare to question the Buddha.

Thereupon, Mañjuśrī rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and reported the aforementioned matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One asked Vimalaprabha,
"Is it truly so? He replied:
"It is truly so," the Buddha told the bhikṣu.
"Did you originally have the intention to commit sexual misconduct?"
He replied, “No,
Blessed One.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"You originally had no intention; how then did you commit this offense?
The bhikṣu replied, "It was only at a later time that the desire arose within me."
“Is it thus, bhikṣu?
Does the mind commit the offense of desire? He replied:
"So it is," the Buddha told the bhikṣus.
"Have I not always said that because the mind is defiled, sentient beings are defiled; and because the mind is pure, sentient beings are pure?"
He replied, "It is so.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"What do you think?
When you were experiencing desire within a dream, was your mind aware of it?
He replied:
"Awakened awareness," the Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"When you previously committed an act of desire, was it not through the mind that you became aware of it?"
He replied, “It is so.
[The Buddha said: “If it is so, bhikṣu!
"What difference is there between committing an act of lust while awake and while dreaming?
The bhikṣu replied,
"There is no difference between committing an act of lust while awake and while dreaming."
The Buddha said,
"What do you think?
Have I not already stated that all phenomena are like dreams?"
He replied, “It is so. The Buddha said:
"What do you think?
Are those dharmas that are like a dream real?
He replied:
"No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"What do you think?"
"Are both the mind in the waking state and the mind in the dream state equally real? "No,
World-Honored One."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If it is not real, is it a dharma that exists? "No, sir."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu:
“What do you think?”
“Does a non-existent dharma arise? “No,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"If a dharma is unarisen, could it have cessation, bondage, or liberation? "No, sir."
“World-Honored One.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
“What do you think?”
"Would dharmas that are unarisen fall into the Avīci Hell, among the hungry ghosts, or among the animals?
He replied:
"World-Honored One!"
"If even the dharma of non-arising does not exist at all, how could there be falling into the three evil realms?
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"The intrinsic nature of all dharmas is pure."

However, all ordinary beings—foolish, small-minded, and lacking wisdom—do not know things as they truly are because dharmas do not exist; thus, they give rise to false conceptualizations, and by virtue of these conceptualizations, they fall into the three evil realms.
Again, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"All dharmas are without reality, yet they manifest various functions that ought to be performed; it is for the sake of ordinary persons who are attached to greed, hatred, and delusion that one discriminates among all dharmas."
Because they are not as they appear, they are not real.
He further addressed the bhikṣus:
“All dharmas are deceptive, for they are like a mirage.”
All phenomena are like dreams, for their intrinsic nature is spontaneously and inherently pure.
All phenomena are ultimate, being like the moon reflected in water, bubbles, and the like.
All phenomena are tranquil, being free from the afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
All phenomena are without grasping, for they are not material dharmas and are invisible.
All phenomena are without accumulation, for they are like empty space.
All phenomena are without intrinsic nature, for they transcend all natures.
All phenomena are profoundly deep, for they transcend empty space.
All phenomena are vast and expansive, for they have no location.
Phenomena are without action, for they are ultimately quiescent.
Dharmas have no basis, for their objective spheres are empty.
Dharmas have no root, for they are ultimately empty.
Dharmas are free from the veils and entanglements, for afflictions, fetters, and proclivities cannot be apprehended.
Phenomena are free from burning, for their nature is non-arising.
Phenomena are without obstruction, for their fundamental nature is pure.
All phenomena are without retribution, for they are like reflections.
All phenomena are like illusions, for they do not accord with suchness.
Phenomena have no basis, for they arise from false discrimination.
All phenomena undergo transmigration, yet sentient beings cling to various extremes.
All phenomena do not arise, because their respective conditions are mutually contradictory in nature.
Phenomena are without defiled attachment, because they have no point of belonging.
Phenomena are without impurity, because all fetters and afflictions are unattainable.
All phenomena are stainless, for their purity exceeds that of space.
Phenomena have no subtle marks, for their marks are quiescent.
All phenomena are harmonious and supple, for their nature is non-arising.
All phenomena are suchness, because there is no distinction between their beginning, middle, and end.
All phenomena are liberation, because they are not mutually bound.
All phenomena are without hearing, being like shards of pottery.
All phenomena are non-material, for they are identical to empty space.
All phenomena are equal, for they have no accumulation.
Phenomena cannot be grasped, just as empty space cannot be seized.
All phenomena are unattainable, for the wise, upon investigation, find them to be unobtainable.
Phenomena are without agitation, for they are pure throughout the three periods of time.
Phenomena are without fetters, for they destroy the darkness of ignorance.
The Dharma is without thorns, for it is free from all entanglements.
All phenomena are peaceful and secure, like nirvana.
The Dharma is without fear, for it has transcended all terrors.
Dharmas have no further shore, because they have no this shore.
All dharmas are immeasurable, because they transcend calculation.
All dharmas are signless, because their signs are empty.
All phenomena are without action, for they sever all aspirations.
All phenomena are without activity, for activity is deceptive.
Phenomena are without conceptual proliferation, for discursive thought and investigation have been extinguished.
The Dharma has no cave or dwelling, for it is free from any place of abiding.
The Dharma has no turbidity, for it is eternally pure.
The Dharma is identical to nirvāṇa; arising cannot be apprehended, for it is empty and non-existent.

"Monks, you should know that all phenomena are thus ineffable. Therefore, when I sat at the site of enlightenment in the past, I attained that which is non-attainment; there is not a single phenomenon that has arising or ceasing, nor one that is bound or liberated, nor is there any phenomenon that is obstructed or entangled, or subject to sorrow or regret."
"Why is this? Because all phenomena are pure and free from defilement.

At that time, Vimalaprabha, hearing this teaching, felt his heart leap with joy; grief and delight mingled within him. Immediately shedding tears, he joined his palms in reverence and gazed one-pointedly upon the Buddha, speaking these verses:
"How wonderful is the World-Honored One’s great merit, To whom gods and worldlings alike turn for refuge!
He has perfectly awakened to all wondrous and supreme practices; I prostrate to him who is able to sever all suffering."
To those without refuge, you provide refuge; to those without a guide, you act as their guide.
Abiding securely in the true path, ever pure—homage to the World-Honored One of Great Majestic Virtue.
You act as a lamp of illumination for the world’s darkness; you provide eyes for those who are sightless.
You are able to deliver those deeply attached to falsehoods. I bow my head to you, the courageous one of great diligence.
Having already abandoned defilements and being free from ill will, you have attained liberation from all fetters and attachments;
equal toward both enemies and kin, you can untie their bonds—to you, the mass of true merit, I prostrate.
Having dried up craving, thirst, and delusion, You have shattered all states of existence and eliminated all suffering;
The cycle of birth and death has long since been severed— I prostrate to the Great Power of the Unsurpassed Vehicle.
Unattached to all conceptual constructions, possessing inconceivable and wondrous wisdom of liberation,
most excellent in the three realms and free from all defilements— I bow my head to you, the pure and stainless person.
I now seek this very path in its entirety, to liberate sentient beings who lack refuge from their suffering;
may I attain such a vehicle, never resorting to the Lesser Vehicle to exhaust all outflows.
For immeasurable billions of nayutas of kalpas, you have constantly endured manifold sufferings without forsaking the Way;
like the full moon manifesting all the stars, I behold the Tathāgata in this same way.
It is like a person who enters the great ocean with an inferior mind seeking only crystal;
though they encounter an immeasurable heap of precious jewels, they discard them to take up that which is base and lowly.
Just as a person who hears of the Buddha’s immeasurable power Does not give rise to the thought,
"I shall attain it," But abandons the vast and extensive deeds of the Mahāyāna To realize the fruit of a śrāvaka instead of awakening.
For example, suppose there is a person who sees a great king surrounded by his various ministers;
yet, instead of seeking the rank of king, they long only for the position of a minister. You should know that such an intention is not wise.
Just as a person who hears of the Buddha’s great merits and the deeds performed through his wondrous and supreme wisdom,
yet finds joy and delight in the Lesser Vehicle— this is indeed a base and indolent mind.
Sentient beings should not crave the Lesser Vehicle, for it is like the light of a firefly in the dark night;
they should instead long for the sunlight that shines everywhere, which is able to destroy all darkness.
The Buddha possesses immeasurable and great renown; his voice reaches throughout the realms of humans, devas, and all evil destinies.
The Buddha’s light is subtle and wondrous, being supreme among all, for it can illuminate every darkness within the world.
For example, like a lion dwelling among jackals, whose mind takes pleasure in the company of jackals,
it abandons what a lion ought to do and instead pursues the ways of jackals.
If there are those among the śrāvakas who act like a great man, yet are like a lion among jackals,
finding satisfaction in delighting in inferior dharmas— know that such people walk the path of poverty.
If one wishes to seek the path of the Mahāyāna, One should always give rise to such a mind:
To benefit the world and sever all suffering; One should not be like those śrāvakas.

At that time, having heard the verses spoken by Vimalaprabha, forty-two thousand devaputras resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. They immediately scattered great *mandārava* flowers, *kumuda* flowers, and others as offerings to the World-Honored One and Mañjuśrī, and praised Vimalaprabha, saying these words:
"Excellent, excellent!"
“Vimalā! You are able to repay the Buddha’s kindness and will bring great benefit to the path of bodhi.
At that moment, the World-Honored One smiled.

It is the constant law of all Buddhas that when they smile, light of five colors issues from their mouths—namely blue, yellow, red, white, and the color of crystal—which illuminates immeasurable and boundless worlds as far as the Brahma-world, eclipsing the radiance of both the sun and the moon; this light then returns to the Buddha, circles him three times, and disappears into the crown of his head.
At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"For what cause and condition do you manifest a smile?
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not manifest a smile without a reason.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This bhikṣu Vimalaprabha possesses great and profound wisdom; having resolved his mind upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I shall now bestow upon him the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"This bhikṣu Vimalaprabha shall attain the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) in the presence of Maitreya Buddha in a future age, and he shall also make offerings to and behold the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa."
After this, having passed ten more kalpas and made offerings to twenty billion buddhas, he attained buddhahood, receiving the name Tathāgata Guṇakamalavara-viśeṣacaryā-siṃhagarjitasvara.
He further addressed Ānanda:

“The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Guṇakamalavara-vicāra-siṃhaghoṣa, that Buddha’s world is named Immeasurable Sound (Anantaghoṣa); it is composed of the seven precious jewels and contains no pratyekabuddhas or śrāvaka disciples, being inhabited solely by bodhisattvas.”
In that Buddha-world, the wheel of Dharma—equal, non-retrogressive, and ever-turning—is constantly turned. Ānanda!
This Vimalaprabha shall soon attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Why is this? It is because he has mounted the wondrous, supreme, and pure Buddha-field.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda:
“Just as wherever the light of the sun reaches, it dispels all darkness, so too, Ānanda!
If there are sentient beings who hear this sutra, you should know that in those places there is great illumination, which enables sentient beings to attain non-obstruction regarding all dharmas.”
At that time, Ānanda came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How do sentient beings attain non-obstruction regarding all dharmas?"
The Buddha said: "Stop, Ānanda!"
"What is the use of asking about such matters?
If the Tathāgata were to speak of obstructions and the absence of obstructions, all gods and people of the world would surely be struck with alarm and doubt.
At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We pray that you will explain the dharmas that constitute obstacles and those that do not.
Upon hearing this, all bodhisattvas will, in the future, during the evil world of the five turbidities, be able to remain free from defiled attachment to worldly dharmas.”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"As for obstacles, lust is an obstacle, hatred is an obstacle, and delusion is an obstacle."
Generosity is an obstruction; ethical discipline is an obstruction; patience is an obstruction; diligence is an obstruction; meditative concentration is an obstruction; and wisdom is an obstruction.
The perception of the Buddha is an obstacle; the perception of the Dharma is an obstacle;
the perception of the Sangha is an obstacle. The perception of emptiness is an obstacle; the perception of signlessness is an obstacle; the perception of wishlessness is an obstacle.
The perception of non-action is an obstacle; the perception of non-arising is an obstacle. Mañjuśrī!
To speak in brief, if one regards any phenomena as being bound or liberated, know that all such things are obstacles.
At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
why are giving, precept-keeping, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom considered obstructive dharmas?”
The Buddha addressed the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī:

"The nature of all dharmas is without obstruction; yet, ordinary people, being foolish, immature, and lacking wisdom, give rise to conceptual discriminations, thereby creating obstructions regarding generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom."
Why is this so? Mañjuśrī!

When ordinary, foolish people practice giving, they do not give rise to reverence toward stingy sentient beings. Because they lack reverence, they give rise to a mind of anger; and because of that angry mind, they fall into the great hells.

One personally upholds the precepts, yet looks upon those who violate them with contempt; one speaks of their faults and evils so that others may hear them and develop a lack of respect, and because of this lack of respect, one falls into the evil realms.
One may personally cultivate patience, yet because of that patience, give rise to a haughty mind, thinking:
"I am patient, while others are coarse and evil.
Because of this patience, one becomes negligent; you should know that this is the very root of all transgressions.
Practicing diligence oneself, one should form this thought toward those who are indolent:
"Such a foolish person should not consume the offerings of others' faithful charity, nor even accept a single drink of water."
"Those who constantly give rise to arrogance toward themselves and disparage others should be known as a foolish and ignorant lot.
While practicing meditative concentration themselves, when they see those with distracted thoughts, they give rise to this thought:
'I always cultivate concentration, whereas these other bhikṣus have many distracted minds and speak of false doctrines.'"
"Such a person is still far removed from the Way; how could they attain Buddhahood?

While entertaining such thoughts, for every single thought that arises, one undergoes birth and death for an eon. Having undergone birth and death, one must then once again cultivate the path to Bodhi.

Relying on their own extensive learning, they give rise to false discrimination regarding nameless phenomena through untruthful wisdom; seeing that things have arisen, they conceive great arrogance, thinking:
"I declare these people to be greatly deluded and ignorant, obscured by various perceptions, and not true men."
"Furthermore, although they aspire to seek the path of the Mahāyāna and speak thus:
'I shall become the most supreme in the world,' they do not give rise to respect for those of the Śrāvaka Hīnayāna;
instead, they treat them with contempt, disdain, and loathing, speaking of their faults and transgressions. Because they utter coarse words with such an evil mind, they fall into the evil destinies."
At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
A bodhisattva should not falsely proclaim the faults of others within the Buddha-dharma.”
The Buddha said: “So it is, so it is, Mañjuśrī!”
"What do you think?
Does a bodhisattva not always give rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, feeling compassion and affection for them, rather than looking upon them with an evil eye?"
Mañjuśrī said: “It is so,
World-Honored One.”
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, what do you think?
Would a bodhisattva ever fail to deliver even a single sentient being by means of the vehicles of the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, or the Mahāyāna?"
“No, World-Honored One.
A bodhisattva has never abandoned even a single sentient being without delivering them, always giving rise to a mind of equanimity toward all.”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"Suppose there is a skilled physician who treats all manner of illnesses for kings, ministers, elders, householders, and even the poor. He constantly thinks to himself:
'How can I enable sentient beings to escape suffering and be freed from all diseases?'"
“Mañjuśrī! It is the same for a bodhisattva, who constantly gives rise to great compassion toward sentient beings and forms an impartial resolve:
‘How may I cause all sentient beings to receive and practice the Buddha-dharma so that it is never interrupted?’”

"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, it is like a skilled physician who, when the medical treatises, scriptures, and incantations he possesses are not lost or interrupted, feels immeasurable joy and exultation in his heart."
The Bodhisattva is also like this: when the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed, the arising of joy in the mind is likewise so.
Mañjuśrī! Not all sentient beings are like a physician who can cure all diseases; even those who possess such ability are difficult to find.
Mañjuśrī! It is the same for a bodhisattva:
they do not adorn themselves by generating the bodhicitta in a manner that is entirely equal to that of a Buddha; even those who are able to do so are rare to find.
Furthermore, just as a skilled physician should not be indolent in cultivating medical arts regarding various medical treatises, scriptures, and secret techniques,
so too, Mañjuśrī, should a bodhisattva not be indolent in generating the bodhicitta, like one who is weak and ill.

Mañjuśrī! To be self-arisen without a teacher is difficult to attain; to know through oneself rather than from another is also difficult to attain; the wondrous and supreme mind is also difficult to attain; and the practice of the Buddha-dharma is also difficult to attain.
At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva attain purity such that the mind encounters no obstruction regarding all phenomena?”
The Buddha addressed the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, saying:
"If there is a bodhisattva who contemplates that desire is all dharmas, and that hatred and delusion are all dharmas, this is called purifying all karmic obstructions."
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

If there is a bodhisattva who neither gives rise to craving for nor abandons the five desires, but contemplates that the true nature of desire is itself the Buddha-dharma, this is called purifying all karmic obstructions."
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

If there is a bodhisattva who seeks awakening through the five hindrances, and when observing in this way neither finds the five hindrances nor awakening, this is called purifying all karmic obstructions."
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

If there is a bodhisattva who contemplates the nine causes of resentment as being identical to a mind of loving-kindness, and when contemplating and observing these nine causes of resentment, perceives neither another person nor his own self—this is called the supreme loving-kindness, because of the non-apprehension of all phenomena."
The Bodhisattva’s contemplation of patience is likewise so; this is called "purifying all karmic obstructions.

Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, if there is a Bodhisattva who contemplates that violating the precepts is itself non-violation, contemplates that what is not the Vinaya is itself the Vinaya, contemplates that bondage is itself liberation, and contemplates that birth-and-death is itself the realm of Nirvāṇa—this is called "purifying all karmic obstructions."
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

If there is a bodhisattva who contemplates the realm of desire as the very realm of nirvāṇa, and likewise regards hatred and delusion in the same way, this is called purifying all karmic obstructions."
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
If there is a bodhisattva who contemplates all phenomena as being the Buddha-dharma, this is called purifying all karmic obstructions."
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
If there is a bodhisattva who contemplates that all phenomena have no substantial nature or characteristics and possess no root, this is called purifying all karmic obstructions."

"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, if there is a bodhisattva who contemplates stinginess and giving without forming dualistic thoughts; observes precepts and violates precepts without forming dualistic thoughts; harbors anger and practices patience without forming dualistic thoughts; is indolent and exerts diligence without forming dualistic thoughts; has a distracted mind and practices meditative concentration without forming dualistic thoughts; and possesses ignorance and wisdom without forming dualistic thoughts—this is called purifying all karmic obstructions."
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
If there is a bodhisattva who contemplates that all afflictions are themselves the Buddha-dharma, this is called purifying all karmic obstructions."
At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva contemplate all afflictions as being precisely the Buddha-dharma?”
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
“What do you think?
Do you perceive any dharma that can act as a fetter for another dharma?”
He replied,
“No, World-Honored One.”
“Mañjuśrī! What do you think?
Do you perceive any dharma that can bring about the liberation of all dharmas?”
"No, World-Honored One. "Mañjuśrī!"
“How does a bodhisattva attain the patience of non-arising? Mañjuśrī replied,
“All afflictions are themselves the patience of non-arising.”
Why is this so? Because all afflictions share the same nature as empty space.

For this reason, I perceive that all phenomena are without wisdom and without abandonment, without realization and without cultivation; yet ordinary beings, obscured by hindrances, lack the Buddha-dharma, for they perceive the existence of fetters to be severed and the Buddha-dharma to be cultivated.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī!”
He is well able to explain the inexhaustible Dharma. Mañjuśrī!

In the distant past, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Sūryavimalaprabhā Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat.
Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata Sun-Stainless Light has a lifespan of ninety kalpas, and his land is named Fragrant Multitude.
In that Buddha-world, many sentient beings delight in the Lesser Dharma, while few are able to practice the unsurpassed Mahāyāna.
After that Buddha, the World-Honored One, had entered parinirvāṇa, the Dharma remained for a thousand years and his relics were distributed, no different from what will occur after my own extinction.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Yongshe (Vīradatta), who was modest, delighted in study, and well-cultivated in the aggregate of ethical discipline; he was learned, possessed wisdom, and was handsome of countenance, having achieved the foremost pure and wondrous complexion.

At that time, Vīradatta put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city of Duṣprasaha; proceeding in order to beg for food, he arrived at the house of an elder. In that household was a daughter of upright and beautiful countenance who had not yet been married to a husband.
At that time, the daughter of the elder saw Vīradatta and conceived a heart of passionate attachment, thinking to herself:
"If I do not obtain the bhikṣu Vīradatta as my husband, I shall take my own life."
At first, he did not speak of such thoughts to anyone; his desire became bound within him and eventually turned into illness.
At that time, Vīradatta, having finished his almsround, returned to the vihāra.
Later, when the girl’s father passed away, her mother asked her,
"For what reason have you fallen ill?
At that time, the girl remained silent and ceased eating and drinking.
At that time, the girl’s mother secretly dispatched another woman—one who had previously been close to her and shared in her joys and sorrows—to go and ask:
"By what causes and conditions has this illness come upon you?"
The woman then replied:
"Previously, I saw a bhikṣu of handsome appearance and immediately conceived a lustful desire, which led to this illness.
If my wish is granted, my illness will be cured; if it is not, I shall surely perish."
At that time, when the other women heard this matter, they returned and recounted the preceding events in detail to their mother.
Having heard this, the mother reflected:
"Now my daughter’s illness is such as this; if she cannot obtain the bhikṣu Vīradatta, what plan should I devise?"
He further thought:
"I should now invite the bhikṣu Vīradatta to come to my house frequently, so that this girl may receive the teachings and the Dharma from him.
At that time, on another occasion, Vīradatta entered the city to beg for alms and arrived at her house once again.
Seeing that the elder’s daughter was emaciated and weak, he asked her,
"For what reason does this girl have such an illness?
At that time, her mother replied:
"But this daughter of mine loves to listen to the Dharma;
I have always firmly obstructed her, preventing her from fulfilling her desire, which has resulted in this illness.
At that time, Yongs-sbyin (Vīradatta) said to his mother:
"Do not obstruct this woman so that she cannot hear the Dharma.
The mother returned and reported,
"Venerable One!..."
"If you can teach this girl the Dharma scriptures, I shall grant my permission.
At that time, Vīradatta immediately gave his consent.
His mother then spoke, saying:
"From now on, please come to my home regularly.
He replied, "I shall do so."
At that time, having heard these words, the daughter of the elder was greatly delighted in her heart and thought:
"I shall now employ various skillful means to cause this bhikṣu to develop attachment toward me."
Then the daughter of the elder said to Vīradatta:
"I pray only that, O Venerable One,
out of compassion for me, you will constantly come to my house."
At that time, Vīradatta silently gave his consent and accepted the food, returning to the monastery.
Then his mother said to his daughter:
"From this day forward, you must adorn yourself well; anoint your body with fine sandalwood and various blended perfumes, and put on fresh, excellent, and exquisite garments."
"Such adornments may be obtained according to one's wishes.

Subsequently, Vīradatta went to her house frequently, and as they grew increasingly intimate through their repeated meetings, he lost his right mindfulness and gave rise to lustful thoughts. He then engaged in sexual intercourse with her; his mind became deeply attached, and he visited her with increasing frequency.
At that time, the husband of that woman, seeing that this bhikṣu came and went so frequently, conceived a sense of suspicion and anger; he immediately devised a stratagem intending to take his life.
Having heard of this matter, the bhikṣu Yongs-sbyin (Vīradatta) thought to himself:
"I shall provide her with poisoned medicine and cause her to end her husband's life."
At that time, Vīradatta immediately took some poison and gave it to her, saying to her:
"If you truly think of me, you may take this medicine and kill your husband."
At that time, the daughter of the elder immediately mixed poison into the food and commanded her maidservant:
"Take this meal and feed it to my husband.
After the husband had eaten the meal, he died instantly.
At that time, having heard that he had passed away, Vīradatta felt great remorse and thought to himself:
"What I have done is a most grievous evil.
How can one be called a bhikṣu who practices sexual misconduct and furthermore takes human life?"
"In this state, where shall I now turn for refuge?
He was filled with great anguish and distress, thinking:
"If my life comes to an end, I shall surely fall into the evil realms."
"Who can deliver me from such suffering?
For this reason, he ran in terror from one monastery to another, his robes falling to the ground as he cried out:
"Alas! How strange! How terrible!"
"I am now indeed a being in hell.

At that time, there was a vihāra named He-mu (Haimavat), in which there was a bodhisattva named Bi-niu-duo-lo (Vinayadatta). The bhikṣu Yongshi immediately entered his room and threw his entire body to the ground.
Then that bodhisattva asked Vīradatta:
"Why have you cast yourself upon the ground?
He replied:
"Venerable One!
I am now indeed a being in hell.
He asked again:
"Who has caused you to become a person of the hells?
Vīradatta replied, "I committed great sins;
I violated the precept against sexual misconduct and also took human life."
Then that bodhisattva said to Śūradatta:
"Bhikṣu, do not be afraid.
I am now able, by my power, to bestow fearlessness upon you."
At that time, having heard the voice of that bodhisattva bestowing fearlessness, the mind of Vīradatta was filled with immeasurable joy and exultation.
Thereupon, the bodhisattva Ghr̥tapradīpa immediately raised Vīradatta from the ground, took him by his right hand, and led him to another place to sit among the trees of a grove.
Then the Bodhisattva Ghr̥tapradīpa rose into the air to the height of one tala tree and said to Śūradatta:
"Do you now have deep faith in me?"
Vīradatta immediately joined his palms in reverence and replied,
"In seeing you, O Benevolent One, I am as if meeting a Great Teacher,
even as I would the World-Honored One. At that moment, the Bodhisattva Ghr̥tapradīpa entered the Tathāgata-Ratnamudrā-Samādhi, the wondrous gateway of the Mahāyāna realm of all Buddhas.

Having entered into samādhi, he immediately manifested immeasurable Buddha-bodies from his own person; all were golden in color and possessed the thirty-two marks, pervading the space between the forest trees.
At that time, all these Buddhas simultaneously spoke these verses with one voice:
"All phenomena are like reflections in a mirror, And also like the moon in the water."
The deluded minds of ordinary beings discriminate through ignorance, anger, and craving.
Phenomena are without action and without location; they are pure like space, devoid of cognition, deceptive, and lacking solidity.
When seeking anger or love within, one never finds them.
Ordinary people give rise to defiled attachment, yet in reality there is no such clinging;
it is like being attached to various forms within a dream while asleep.
Just as when a knife cuts an object, the knife has no cognition;
so it is with ordinary people: deluded and ignorant, they engage in false discrimination, giving rise to defiled attachment toward craving and increasing contention through anger.
The world is like a dream, empty and without solidity;
like a mirage or clouds in the sky, delusion and craving are tranquil and signless.
All phenomena are like grass and trees; the mind exists neither within nor without.
Craving is not the life-span or the person; its intrinsic nature is non-existent.
When ordinary beings perceive all phenomena, they reckon them as arising from causes and conditions;
yet they are uncreated and cannot be grasped, for their nature is detached and eternally quiescent.
All phenomena are like illusions, yet ordinary beings give rise to grasping and attachment;
the nature of illusion is without solidity, and so it is with greed, hatred, and delusion.
All phenomena are eternally signless, quiescent, and without foundation.
Boundless and ungraspable, the nature of desire is likewise.
Sentient beings are like reflections; they cling to "mine," yet apart from such false conceptualization, there is nothing solid to be grasped.
All phenomena are like shadows and echoes; desire and anger have no abode.
Like illusions, dreams, and the moon reflected in water, there is truly no one who is stained by or subject to anger.
Objects of perception are not real; they are empty, non-existent, and ungraspable.
Discriminating phenomena have no master; their root is eternally quiescent.
Like a conjured person, they possess no greed, hatred, or delusion.
All phenomena such as illusions and dreams—no limit to them can be found.
Like the moon appearing in water, yet not being within the water;
so too are ordinary beings stained by delusion and anger—yet this delusion, craving, and anger have no inherent nature;
they are but greed, hatred, and ignorance.
All conditions are eternally empty and non-existent; there is no sentient being, no life-span.
They are void and eternally quiescent; there is neither eye nor ear, and the nose and tongue are likewise so.
Fools are deluded and lack wisdom, clinging tenaciously to what is false and illusory.
Just as space is boundless, Inexhaustible, and without coming or going,
So too are all phenomena, Like a hand reaching into empty space.
Though there are various conceptualizations of phenomena, In reality, there is no one who conceptualizes.
Fools conceive of the aggregates, yet in reality there is no arising.
As I contemplate all phenomena, their nature and characteristics are non-existent;
they neither arise nor cease, and have never undergone aggregation or dispersion.
"The nature of all phenomena is liberation; it is quiescent and has no location.
There is no one who can grasp or take it up; to understand this is called wisdom.

At that time, the twelve thousand devaputras in the forest who had come to the Bodhisattva Gandhahastin to hear the Dharma, upon hearing these verses, immediately attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

When the bhikṣu Vīradatta beheld the supernatural manifestations and transformations of the emanated buddhas, he contemplated and discerned among all phenomena; thereby, free from all hindrances and entanglements, he attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
“Mañjuśrī! Do not give rise to doubt.
Who else could that Bodhisattva Ghoṣadatta have been at that time? It was none other than you.”
The present Maitreya Bodhisattva is he.
As for the bhikṣu Vīradatta, could he be anyone else?
He is the Tathāgata Ratnacandra.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
has the bhikṣu Vīradatta already attained Buddhahood?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “He has already attained Buddhahood;

to the west of this buddha-field, beyond as many buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, there is a land named Constant Light, where the Tathāgata Ratnacandra has attained buddhahood.”

Mañjuśrī! Observe this Dharma, which can cause sentient beings to be free from all karmic obstructions; even those who engage in sexual misconduct or take the lives of others can, through it, attain the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti) in their present bodies.
Why is this? Because they are able to contemplate the three realms as being like shadows and echoes.
It is just as a magician views a conjured person without any hindrance.

Mañjuśrī! All ordinary persons falsely give rise to conceptual discrimination regarding dharmas that do not exist; they thus fall into the various evil destinies and undergo immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of sufferings.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there are bodhisattvas who, upon hearing this sutra, receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, make offerings to, revere, and praise it, what benefits will they obtain in their present life?”
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
“What do you think?
When the light of the sun shines upon Jambudvīpa, how much benefit does it bring to sentient beings?”
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Just as the light of the sun shines upon Jambudvīpa, bringing benefit to all sentient beings in ways that are immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable.”
“Mañjuśrī! You should know that this sutra is also like this:

it can cause bodhisattvas to break all fetters and bonds, give rise to immeasurable light of wisdom, and attain non-obstruction regarding all dharmas; it can swiftly produce unhindered wisdom and eloquence, such that when preaching the Dharma, one cannot be defeated by various māras or externalists, nor have one’s joy in teaching interrupted.”
Mañjuśrī! Just as a great fire consumes grasses and trees without leaving a trace, you should know that this sutra likewise burns away all fetters.

Mañjuśrī! Just as the king of snowy mountains cannot be obscured by any other black mountains, so it is with a bodhisattva who hears this sutra: no other heterodox practitioners can rightfully destroy them.
Mañjuśrī! Just as no minor kings dare to resist or oppose a wheel-turning monarch, so it is with a bodhisattva who has heard this sutra:
no one can suppress such a person, including those who engage in various treatises or adorn their speech with ornate phrases.
Mañjuśrī! Just as a bhikṣu who is well-versed in the Vinaya can eliminate the doubts and regrets regarding broken precepts in others,
you should know that this sutra is likewise able to cause sentient beings to be free from all sorrow and regret.
Mañjuśrī! Just as wherever the Sun Deva arrives he is able to destroy all darkness, so too it is for a bodhisattva who hears this sutra:
they are able to destroy all the black darkness of ignorance and are able to give rise to the radiance of all wisdom.
"Why is this? It is because wisdom has been well-cultivated by means of this sutra.
At that time, Māra the Evil One came to where the Buddha was and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata, out of great compassion, pities all beings and constantly bestows peace and happiness upon them.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will not preach this sūtra.”
Why is this? If this sutra is preached, the palaces of all the Māras will tremble, and the arrows of grief and affliction will enter my body.
World-Honored One, it is because this scripture shall circulate throughout Jambudvīpa.

I shall now cause it to be so that there will be no one who receives, upholds, reads, recites, copies, or makes offerings to such a sutra as this; I shall make this sutra appear like a heterodox path, causing sentient beings to give rise to false views, and leading the bhikṣus who read and recite the Vaipulya Mahāyāna to feel doubt, regret, and slander toward this sutra.

At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, immediately prostrated himself before the Buddha with his head at the Buddha’s feet, scattered heavenly māndārava flowers over the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Māra Pāpīyān will employ various skillful means to create obstacles for this sutra.
World-Honored One!
I shall receive, uphold, read, recite, transcribe, make offerings to, and revere it.
After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, Ānanda and I shall cause this sutra to circulate throughout Jambudvīpa, ensuring it spreads everywhere.
I, along with the Four Heavenly Kings and the various spirits and deities, shall constantly provide protection for those who preach this sutra.
"If there are those who receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, make offerings to, and revere this sutra, I shall be their principal protector among all guardians.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, make offerings to, and revere such a sutra as this, and you should also disseminate and manifest it for others."
Why is this so? Ānanda!
This sutra is the mirror of all dharmas.
Ānanda said: "As the World-Honored One has instructed, I shall receive and uphold it.
What should this sutra be named?"
"How should one practice it?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This sutra is named 'Purification of All Karmic Obstructions,' and it is also named 'Entering the Unobstructed Wisdom of All Dharmas.'"

While this sutra was being spoken, sixty bhikṣus attained the exhaustion of outflows through the liberation of mind by not grasping at any dharmas; eighty bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, as well as the devas, humans, gandharvas, asuras, and others, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced, and they faithfully accepted and practiced it.
The Sūtra on Purifying Karmic Obstructions Spoken by the Buddha.
